name: Pattern 5: Early Warning, Then a Person Reaches Out
title: Pattern 5: Early Warning, Then a Person Reaches Out
answer: Pattern 5 is an early warning approach in which attendance, grades, behavior records, and screening results are combined into a flag that prompts a person to look closer at a student who may be slipping. The flag itself is only the beginning: a counselor, teacher, or attendance officer then contacts the family, talks with the student, and works out what is really happening. It matters because the strongest evidence in this Volume sits here, yet the pattern depends far more on human follow up than on AI.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: This pattern solves the problem of a student drifting off course before anyone notices. Data from several routine sources are brought together so that a possible slip shows up as a flag rather than staying invisible. The flag does not decide anything on its own; it tells someone that a closer look is warranted. From there a counselor, teacher, or attendance officer reaches out to the family and the student to understand the real situation. The pattern therefore pairs a signal with a human response rather than replacing the response with a prediction.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, the flag is generated from attendance, grades, behavior records, and screening results, and it routes to a named person who follows up. That person calls the family, speaks with the student, and tries to find out what is actually going on. The text gives grade band detail mainly for the early grades, where a trial cut chronic absence by 15 percent, and it notes that newer district trials found smaller effects of around 2 percent. The same follow up logic applies wherever the flag appears, since the pattern always ends with a person rather than a model. Districts are also asked in Chapter 18 to publish the indicators they use so families can see what drives a flag.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this as some of the strongest evidence in the Volume, and notes that it involves very little AI. In a large randomized trial, personalized mailings telling parents exactly how many days their child had missed cut chronic absence by 10 percent or more, largely because parents had underestimated the number (Rogers & Feller, 2018). A second trial in the early grades cut chronic absence by 15 percent (Robinson et al., 2018). Newer trials run by districts found smaller effects of around 2 percent, which the text describes as still real at low cost (Berger et al., 2025).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets out clear limits. Prediction models can carry bias, and people tend to read unclear results through the beliefs they already hold (Soland et al., 2020). Models also miss the events that actually push a student off course, such as a family move, a health problem, or a new job. That is why the pattern always ends with a person, and why Chapter 18 asks districts to publish the indicators they use so families can see what drives a flag. The decisions about what a flag means and what to do next stay with the people who reach out.
